title: Create and Operate Scheduled Jobs
readerIntent: Create a safe tenant-owned scheduled job and operate it through restart, failure, and recovery.
priorKnowledge: Understand services, service identity, tenant context, and runtime topology.
owner: CronJob owns scheduling and lifecycle; the selected handler or target module owns business behavior
summary: Define an approved persisted job, implement business work in its owning service, assign eligible node placement, secure lifecycle commands, and prove idempotency, overlap, retry, restart, and reconciliation.

sections.heading: Example: reconcile stock reservations
paragraphs: Suppose an ecommerce project must find expired stock reservations every five minutes and release them. Inventory owns reservation rules and updates. CronJob owns when the approved Inventory handler runs; it does not reimplement reservation logic.

sections.heading: 1. Design the contract
items: Choose a stable tenant-scoped job code, business owner, schedule and timezone, active state, start/end window, priority, normal runOnNode, and optional qualified failover policy.
Name the approved owning handler or target-module operation; never accept arbitrary service names, URLs, credentials, node identifiers, or executable code from untrusted request data.
Define timeout, maximum concurrency, overlap behavior, retry count/backoff, idempotency key, duplicate policy, retention, quarantine, reconciliation, compensation, and alert thresholds.

Decide whether a workflow or event is more appropriate: use Workflow for durable multi-step/manual business processes and events for decoupled facts; do not hide those responsibilities in a cron handler.

sections.heading: 2. Implement in the owning project module
items: Contribute the job definition and configuration through a later project module so framework CronJob remains reusable.
Implement reservation discovery and release in Inventory services using its schema models, validation, authorization, and persistence contracts.
Keep the scheduled handler bounded and resumable; process records in pages and persist enough progress or idempotency state to recover safely.
When the job calls another module, use the tenant-scoped internal service-token flow and satisfy that module's route permission. Never store or reuse an employee username/password.

sections.heading: 3. Register and run
items: Import or create the definition through the governed CronJob contracts; startup side effects must not create duplicates.
An eligible CronJob module instance builds its disposable local schedule from the persisted definition when runOnNode or approved tempNode matches.
Scheduled and authorized manual runs use the same definition, handler, tenant, eligibility, overlap, evidence, and failure contracts.
A server only hosts active modules; CronJob remains module-owned regardless of consolidated or distributed process placement.

sections.heading: 4. Operate and recover
items: Use secured create, update, run, start, stop, pause, resume, and remove commands; state changes must not use GET.
Monitor due, started, completed, failed, skipped, schedule delay, duration, overlap denial, attempts, node assignment/handoff, downstream latency, stale running state, and reconciliation outcome.
Graceful drain stops acquisition and local schedules while the persisted definition survives; restart rebuilds eligible schedules idempotently.
A timeout, network partition, crash, or node loss may leave the business outcome unknown. Reconcile authoritative Inventory state before retrying or compensating.

sections.heading: Verification
items: Positive schedule and manual run; invalid definition; inactive job; unauthorized, wrong-token-type, and cross-tenant access.
Start/end and timezone boundaries; duplicate definition; concurrent trigger; overlap denial; timeout; safe and unsafe retry; pagination; rate/capacity limits.
Restart, drain, hard termination, node loss/return, delayed failure detection, downstream outage/recovery, temporary ownership, idempotency, reconciliation, and compensation.
Contract, integration, modular topology, observability/redaction, performance, upgrade, and regression evidence.

sections.heading: Complete guide: How To Create Scheduled Jobs
paragraphs: Scheduled jobs are automated tasks that run at configured times.
Examples:
items: Import files from a trusted location.

sections.heading: Beginner Summary
paragraphs: A scheduled job is used when Nodics must do work without a user clicking a button or calling an API at that moment.
Think of a job as three parts:

| Part | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Definition | What the job is called, when it runs, whether it is active, and which module owns it. |
| Handler | The small runtime function that starts the job work and records lifecycle events. |
| Service | The real business behavior, such as import files, rebuild indexes, or send messages. |
Keep the service testable without waiting for the clock. The schedule triggers the service, but the service owns the business work.

sections.heading: CronJobs
paragraphs: CronJobs are Nodics scheduled tasks with persisted definitions, lifecycle operations, handlers, logs, route/service ownership, node responsibility, and tests.

A CronJob should not be only a timer in memory. It should have a definition that explains what runs, when it runs, who owns it, how it is started or stopped, how failures are recorded, and which server/node may execute it.

sections.heading: When To Use A Scheduled Job
paragraphs: Use a scheduled job when work runs automatically without a user request.
Do not use a scheduled job when:
items: The work must happen immediately inside an API transaction.
The work belongs on an event.
The work belongs to a workflow step.
The work requires manual approval before every run.

sections.heading: What A Job Needs
paragraphs: A scheduled job usually needs:
In Nodics, a scheduled job is a persisted platform capability. The job definition, trigger information, handler/service behavior, logs, and lifecycle state are visible and testable.
![CronJob Process](../assets/images/cron-job-process.jpg)
items: Permission or runtime guard rules when applicable.

sections.heading: Node Ownership
paragraphs: In a multi-node application, not every node runs every job.
Document:
This is important because duplicate scheduled work can create duplicate data, repeated messages, or conflicting updates.
items: Which server or node owns the job.
Whether only one node can run it at a time.
What happens if the node stops during execution.

sections.heading: Job Implementation Pattern
paragraphs: Keep the actual business behavior in a service.
The job triggers the service. The service is testable without waiting for the schedule.
Recommended shape:
items: Job definition identifies when and where the job runs.
Service validates input and tenant context.

sections.heading: Job Lifecycle
paragraphs: A scheduled job usually moves through lifecycle actions:
Each lifecycle action has permission checks, diagnostics, and tests. Repeated startup does not create duplicate jobs.
![CronJob Lifecycle](../assets/images/cron-job-lifecycle.png)
CronJob lifecycle APIs are command APIs. They should use command-safe HTTP methods:
Do not expose lifecycle mutations through `GET`. A `GET` route can be retried, prefetched, cached, or called by monitoring tools as if it were read-only, so it must not change scheduler state.
items: create or register the job definition;
`POST` to create/register, run, start, stop, pause, and resume jobs;
`DELETE` to remove jobs from the runtime scheduler pool.

sections.heading: Creating A New Job
paragraphs: Steps:
items: Decide which capability owns the job.
Add the job definition in that module.
Add or update configuration for the schedule.
Add tests for lifecycle, handler behavior, and node responsibility.
Document how to run, update, and disable the job.

sections.heading: Where To Write Job Code
paragraphs:
| Need | Write here |
| --- | --- |
| Job definition or startup seed data | Owning module data/config area used by CronJob initialization |
| Schedule, enablement, retry, node responsibility | Owning module or server/node `config/properties.js` |
| Business behavior | Owning module `src/service/**/*Service.js` |
| Process hooks around job execution | `src/pipelines`, `src/interceptors`, or `src/event` when the process needs them |
| API lifecycle route changes | CronJob router/controller/facade/service layer |
| Status values or enums | Owning module `src/utils/statusDefinitions.js` or `src/utils/enums.js` |
| Tests | Owning module `test/` plus cronjob route/service/topology tests |
If an AI tool creates a job, ask it to identify each row it touched. If it puts the job body directly in a timer callback, ask it to move the behavior into a service.

sections.heading: Triggers And Handlers
paragraphs: The trigger decides when the job runs. The handler decides what work is executed.
Keep handlers small. A handler resolves context, calls the owning service, and records the result. The service contains the business behavior so it can be tested without waiting for the scheduler.
If a project needs to change a handler, add the override in a later module through the standard service/handler path. Do not edit framework cronjob behavior for one customer requirement.

sections.heading: Generalizing CronJobService
paragraphs: Generalize `CronJobService` behavior when a project needs to change the way jobs are created, scheduled, executed, logged, paused, resumed, retried, or removed while preserving the scheduled-job contract.
When generalizing:
items: avoid duplicate scheduling on repeated startup;
add tests for default and override behavior.

sections.heading: CronJob Handlers
paragraphs: CronJob handlers are lifecycle hooks around scheduled execution. They should resolve context, call the owning service, record results, and pass errors to diagnostics.

sections.heading: handleCronJobStart
paragraphs: Runs when a CronJob starts scheduling or execution. Use it to record start state, prepare context, and confirm the job is allowed to run on the current node.

sections.heading: handleCronJobEnd
paragraphs: Runs when a CronJob ends. Use it to finalize state, release resources, and record completion diagnostics.

sections.heading: handleCronJobPaused
paragraphs: Runs when scheduling is paused. Use it to record paused state and prevent new trigger execution without deleting the job definition.

sections.heading: handleCronJobResumed
paragraphs: Runs when scheduling resumes. Use it to re-enable trigger evaluation and record the resume action.

sections.heading: handleJobTriggered
paragraphs: Runs when the schedule or manual run action triggers the job. Use it to capture trigger time, run id, tenant context, and node ownership before business behavior starts.

sections.heading: handleJobCompleted
paragraphs: Runs after the job work completes. Use it to record result state, duration, output summary, and follow-up actions such as events or retries.

sections.heading: handleSuccess
paragraphs: Runs when the job succeeds. Use it to record success-specific diagnostics and cleanup. Do not hide partial failures inside success; if record-level failures occurred, the job result should make that visible.

sections.heading: Generalizing Handlers
paragraphs: Projects may override handlers through later modules when lifecycle behavior needs to change. Handler overrides must preserve lifecycle state, diagnostics, tenant context, node ownership, and failure propagation.

sections.heading: Testing Scheduled Jobs
paragraphs: Run scheduled-job tests through:

```bash
npm run test:suite -- --suite=cronjob
```
The main test gate also includes scheduled-job coverage:

```bash
npm run test:basic
```

sections.heading: Executing or Scheduling CronJobs
paragraphs: CronJobs may run through startup scheduling, API-controlled lifecycle operations, or explicit service-triggered execution when allowed.
Common operations include:

Each operation should be permissioned, tenant-aware where applicable, observable, and tested. Do not execute the same job from multiple nodes unless the job is explicitly designed for parallel execution.

sections.heading: What To Avoid
paragraphs: Avoid:
items: Running the same job on multiple nodes unintentionally.
Hiding job behavior inside configuration only.
Using jobs for work that belongs on an event.
Putting customer-specific job behavior into framework code.

sections.heading: Beginner Troubleshooting
paragraphs:
| Problem | Likely cause | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Job runs twice | More than one node owns the same job | Node responsibility and scheduler container tests |
| Job never runs | Job disabled, wrong schedule, wrong node, or scheduler not started | Job definition, config, lifecycle state, logs |
| Startup creates duplicates | Initializer is not idempotent | Job code uniqueness and startup tests |
| Job succeeds but data is wrong | Business logic is hidden in handler or lacks tenant context | Move behavior to service and test tenant behavior |
| Failure is invisible | Error was swallowed | Logs, result state, diagnostics, failure propagation |
